This article was written by: Thekgo Raseala
Image: Pexels/Kaboompics
El Niño heat can affect various aspects of nature, meaning summer crops and flowers may need extra care and attention. The usual gardening routine may require a few adjustments and a little more effort to help plants thrive during periods of extreme heat.
Here are a few tips to help nurture your veggie garden during extremely hot weather.
Veggie gardens
According to Garden & Home, the weather conditions in which crops grow play an important role in their health, growth and overall quality. High temperatures, however, can put vegetables under heat stress and affect their development. The publication shares a few ways to help minimise heat stress and keep your vegetable garden healthy during hot weather.
Check the moisture of your soil
The soil needs to be moist to provide cooling for the plants, which happens through the evaporation of water from their leaves. So make sure to provide water through irrigation during those hot summer days. Do this at least twice a week.
Image: Pexels
Provide more water than you think necessary
Another way to protect plants from heat stress is by watering deeply. This should be done before the day reaches its peak temperatures. This also encourages plants to develop deeper roots.
Use shade cloth
Shade cloth can be placed over the crops. It provides adequate cooling without blocking too much light for most vegetables. This provides relief from the extreme hot sun rays whilst still receiving the light required for the plants’ nutritional needs.
Image: Pexels
Add mulch
Mulch keeps the soil moist and is important for crops like tomatoes and lettuce, which are super sensitive to heat stress.
Flower gardens
A lot of what was suggested for the crops can be applied to a flower garden; however, two tips are unique to flower care.
Image: Pexels
Avoid fertiliser
According to bobvila.com, fertilisers promote new growth, which means new, delicate flowers. Mature, strong flowers are more likely to survive extreme heat than younger flowers.
Avoid stressing your plants
Avoid pruning, fertilising, and transplanting, as they cause added stress to plants. Under normal circumstances, plants can recover quickly, but during a heat wave, these activities add unnecessary stress that can put plant health at risk.
This article first appeared on Bona.

By Lebone Rodah Mosima
As temperatures soar across Gauteng, residents are being urged to stay hydrated and protect themselves from the heat, while many are struggling to access water from their taps.
On Saturday, water advocacy group WaterCAN said it had received reports of outages and severely reduced water pressure across several communities, with residents in parts of Soweto reporting shortages lasting nearly seven days.
“The causes remain unclear. Low reservoir levels, infrastructure failures, pumping constraints and electricity interruptions are possible contributing factors,” WaterCAN said in a statement.
“Residents have also questioned reports of supply restrictions without adequate explanation from Johannesburg Water.”
WaterCAN said poor communication had left communities uncertain about restoration times and emergency water arrangements.
The situation is particularly concerning during the current heatwave and amid the prospect of El Niño conditions, which could bring hotter and drier weather.
“Extreme heat increases the risk of dehydration and heat exhaustion, particularly among children, older people and vulnerable residents,” WaterCAN said.
“Some households are forced to queue for water, carry containers over long distances or find alternative supplies for cooking, washing and drinking.”
Professor Francois Engelbrecht, a climatology expert at the University of the Witwatersrand’s Global Change Institute, told Inside Metros that El Niño typically brings hotter and drier conditions to southern Africa, although the climate pattern does not follow a rigid rule.
“If you look at the seasonal forecast for the summer, almost every single forecast model in the world is indicating that it will be a dry summer on the average,” Engelbrecht said.
He explained that El Niño does not mean rain will disappear entirely or that every day will be unusually hot. Rather, El Niño summers tend to experience more extremely hot days and below-average rainfall.
Engelbrecht said the region faced an increased risk of drought and extreme heat between October and March, with persistent high-pressure systems suppressing cloud formation and allowing intense sunlight to heat the land.
He warned that recurrent heatwaves, intensified by global warming and El Niño conditions, posed serious health risks, particularly to older people and other vulnerable groups.
However, Engelbrecht said South Africa’s major dams held substantial water reserves, meaning the immediate concern was not necessarily a shortage of raw water but the ability of municipalities to deliver it reliably.
“We go into the summer, our big dams are still almost at 100% full. That was the state at the end of September anyway,” he said.
“So, we’re in a very good position. Even a big drought cannot cause us to run out of water this summer in terms of water being available in the big dams.”
“The problem is not this summer at least that we will not have water available from the dams. The problem is providing the water to people all the time. That’s where we are in big trouble.”
Engelbrecht said ageing infrastructure, leaking pipes and distribution failures could result in frequent outages during periods of high demand, increasing the health risks associated with extreme heat.
While long-term infrastructure repairs would require substantial investment and planning, he said municipalities needed to ensure that water tankers were available to provide immediate relief to affected communities.
He also encouraged residents to conserve water, maintain emergency supplies where possible and assist vulnerable neighbours and family members during heatwaves.
WaterCAN’s Nomsa Daele said the situation raised serious questions about municipal preparedness and accountability.
“Residents should not have to queue for water, carry containers over long distances or rely on rumours to understand why their supply has been interrupted,” Daele said.
“Whatever the operational challenges, municipalities have a responsibility to communicate openly, provide emergency water and ensure that communities are not left without access to this basic necessity.”
“The public deserves to know what is happening, why it is happening and what is being done to restore supply.”
WaterCAN also pointed to the Department of Water and Sanitation’s Monthly Dashboard for a Water Secure Gauteng, dated 30 October 2026, which showed growing pressure on the province’s water infrastructure.
According to the dashboard, nine municipalities collectively consumed 4.305 billion litres of water daily against an efficiency target of 3.604 billion litres, exceeding the target by 701 million litres, or approximately 19%.
Johannesburg recorded the largest excess consumption by volume at 368 million litres daily, followed by Tshwane at 227 million litres.
Tshwane recorded the highest proportional excess at 34%, followed by Emfuleni at 32% and Johannesburg at 27%.
WaterCAN said non-revenue water, which includes leaks and commercial losses, averaged 43.6% across Gauteng’s three metros on an unweighted basis.
Johannesburg recorded 49.8%, Tshwane 46% and Ekurhuleni 35.1%, all exceeding the national target of 25%.
Water storage levels also raised concerns.
Although the Integrated Vaal River System recorded raw-water storage of 98.2% on 26 October, the four main Rand Water reservoir systems supplying Gauteng stood at just 31.1% on 30 October, against an operational target of 60%.
According to WaterCAN, the system had remained above this threshold for only six days during the preceding five months.
The organisation said high raw-water storage did not guarantee reliable household supply because water still needed to be treated, pumped and distributed through functioning infrastructure.
“Infrastructure problems and electricity interruptions have affected pumping operations, particularly at the Vereeniging water treatment plant and Eikenhof booster pump station, which supplies parts of Johannesburg, including Soweto, Roodepoort and Sandton,” WaterCAN said.
It cautioned that while the figures did not establish the causes of individual outages, they exposed serious weaknesses in Gauteng’s water supply system, particularly as extreme heat increased demand.
Daele said climate change and extreme weather were placing additional pressure on already vulnerable infrastructure.
“But the impact of these conditions is shaped by how well our institutions plan, maintain infrastructure and manage water resources,” she said.
“We cannot blame the weather when communities are left without water because of failures that should have been anticipated and addressed. Climate preparedness must start with ensuring that people have reliable access to water.”
She said the prospect of El Niño reinforced the need for contingency plans that accounted for increased demand, infrastructure failures and prolonged interruptions.
Municipalities could no longer afford to treat each disruption as an isolated incident, she added.
WaterCAN called on water services authorities across Gauteng, including Johannesburg, Tshwane, Ekurhuleni and affected local municipalities, to explain the outages, guarantee emergency water supplies, improve communication, protect public health and address systemic infrastructure weaknesses.
Daele stressed that access to water was a constitutional right, not a privilege.
“During extreme heat, it is fundamental to protecting public health,” she said.
“Gauteng’s residents should not have to spend hours searching or queuing for water while being told to stay hydrated.”

An obituary published following the death of 104-year-old Muar matriarch Loo Siew Chin has drawn public attention to a three-generation Malaysian family that produced 45 medical doctors from rubber-tapping roots.
According to the family notice, Madam Loo died on 12 November at 104.
Her funeral service took place today (16 Nov) at 10 AM from Lorong Serkam 1 in Pekan Muar, followed by burial at the Trinity Church Muar Cemetery along Jalan Bakri, with all funeral contributions directed to charity.
Across four columns listing 11 children, 48 grandchildren, 23 grandchildren-in-law, and 51 great-grandchildren, the notice names 39 individuals carrying the “Dr” title, comprising eight of her nine sons, one daughter-in-law, and 30 grandchildren.
According to a previous New Straits Times report, the wider family tally stands at 45 medical doctors—including 20 specialists and a Universiti Malaya (UM) medical associate professor—accounting for spouses and extended descendants whose titles or names were omitted from the printed notice.
While seven brothers carry their father’s Lim surname, the eldest son is listed as Liew Dr Lim Boon Sho and the fifth son as Liew Boon Tat—a traditional Chinese practice of giving sons their mother’s family surname so her side of the family name continues.
Backyard Farming, Red Wine, And A Daughter Dual-Qualified In Law And Accounting
Her eldest son, Datuk Dr Lim Boon Sho, recounted that Madam Loo and her late husband, Lim Tang Too, had no schooling and made a living tapping rubber in Kampung Belemang, Serom.
During the Malayan Emergency, the family moved to Muar to get away from communist rebels who were forcing villagers to pay protection money.
To afford food and hospital visits for the 11 children, the brothers washed vegetables and cleaned fish at local markets on weekends for one to two ringgit.
Lim urged his eldest son to pursue medicine so he could treat his younger siblings, prompting Boon Sho to begin medical studies in India in 1964 before seven of his eight brothers followed the same career path.
Speaking to China Press and Oriental Daily, Boon Sho, a former Sungai Bakap assemblyman, said his mother maintained a daily routine of physical labour in addition to tapping rubber.
According to him, Madam Loo raised chickens, ducks, and piglets beside the family home and grew vegetables, continuing to tend her own vegetable patch even after her children reached adulthood while keeping to a light diet and enjoying occasional glasses of red wine.
He noted that during lean years, she insisted on serving a bowl of porridge to every visitor so no guest left hungry, while her third son, 75-year-old Dr Lim Boon Boh, recalled that she once lent out her only cash savings to an acquaintance in urgent need.
Alongside her eight physician sons, one daughter qualified as both a lawyer and an accountant.
According to Kwong Wah Yit Poh, her descendants now reside across Malaysia, Singapore, Australia, and the United Kingdom, returning to Muar every Lunar New Year in keeping with her directive to preserve sibling unity, avoid disputes over material interests, and contribute to society.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) needs to rise about 95% to reach its all-time high of $126,080, which was set on October 6, 2025. Currently priced at $64,664, Bitcoin is 48.7% below that peak and has dropped 26.1% since the beginning of 2026.
Sellers are still active in the market. On November 14, Bitcoin closed at $64,120, marking the lowest point in a 30-day trading range, which peaked at $84,082 on October 21, a significant 23.7% drop. It has also fallen below its 200-week moving average, a key gauge of long-term price trends. So, when can we expect Bitcoin to bounce back to its all-time high, and what factors could delay this recovery?
Bitcoin Needs a 95% Gain to Reclaim $126,080
With approximately 20.1 million Bitcoins in circulation, achieving a price of $126,080 would mean a market value of around $2.5 trillion. This is nearly double the current market cap of $1.3 trillion.
However, increasing supply complicates Bitcoin’s path to recovery. Miners continue to produce new coins, so maintaining the same price requires more investment. For example, Bitcoin closed at $64,654 on November 13, 2021, with a market cap of about $1.22 trillion. Now, at a similar price of $64,664, its market value has risen to approximately $1.30 trillion.
Moreover, market trends indicate downward momentum. Bitcoin is currently trading below its 20-day average of $75,828, its 50-day average of $80,159, and its 200-day average of $72,982, which are 17.3%, 24%, and 12.9% higher than its current price, respectively.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs, which hold the coin for stock market investors, saw outflows every trading day from November 5 to 13, according to SoSoValue, leading to a 21.1% drop in their net assets from $109.3 billion on October 21 to $86.2 billion.
Past Bitcoin Recoveries Took 9 Months to Nearly Three Years
Bitcoin has experienced significant drops before, and recovery times have varied considerably, often tied to Federal Reserve actions. Our review of the last three major Bitcoin crashes found these recovery times.
2018 bear market. Bitcoin plummeted 84% from $20,000 in December 2017 to $3,200 in December 2018, taking nearly three years to reclaim the $20,000 mark.
2020 COVID crash. A 58% decline quickly reversed after the Fed injected over $4 trillion into the economy. Bitcoin surpassed its 2017 high by December 2020, about nine months after hitting its lowest point.
2022 collapse. After a 77% drop from $69,000 in November 2021, as the Fed raised rates by 525 basis points, Bitcoin took 28 months to reach a new all-time high in March 2024.
Currently, the situation resembles the 2022 collapse due to the Fed’s ongoing rate hikes. With the target rate rising to 4% on September 16 and another meeting scheduled for December 9, Bitcoin may face another lengthy recovery. A similar 28-month wait from the October 2025 peak could see Bitcoin hit new highs around early 2028.
Bernstein, Standard Chartered and ARK See Prices Above $126,080
Despite the downturn, several analysts still predict higher Bitcoin prices, though most of these calls came before the latest slide.
Bernstein. A research note from August projected Bitcoin reaching $125,000 by December 31 and $150,000 by mid-2027, connecting these targets to Bitcoin’s four-year cycle following each halving.
Alex Thorn. Galaxy’s head of research maintained his $250,000 target by the end of 2027, calling a return to around $125,000 “pretty conservative.”
Standard Chartered. The bank revised its expectations but still anticipates Bitcoin could hit $500,000 by 2030.
ARK Invest. The firm forecasts a central price of $710,000 by 2030, with an optimistic estimate reaching as high as $1.5 million.
Bitcoin also appears to have less distance to cover than other major cryptocurrencies. Our September analysis of which coin gets back first suggested Bitcoin could rebound more quickly, needing only a 49% rise.
Bitcoin All-Time High FAQ
Will Bitcoin Go Back Up?
Historically, all Bitcoin declines of over 40% have eventually led to new highs. However, in the short term, Bitcoin is trading below its 20-day, 50-day, and 200-day averages, suggesting sellers have the short-term advantage.
Will Bitcoin Recover?
We believe Bitcoin could reclaim $126,080, likely in 2028. However, if the weekly closing price falls below the June 30 low of $58,566, it could push this timeline back.
How High Will Bitcoin Go in 2027?
Bernstein forecasts $150,000 by mid-2027, while Thorn cites a target of $250,000 by year-end. Testing the all-time high in 2027 is feasible, but surpassing $150,000 that year seems unlikely.
What Is a Realistic Bitcoin Price by 2030?
Standard Chartered’s target of $500,000 and ARK’s forecast of $710,000 are on the high end. Our analysis suggests a low- to mid-six-figure price is reasonable, while predictions of $1 million appear overly ambitious.
So, When Will Bitcoin Reclaim Its All-Time High?
We predict 2027 could be the earliest year for Bitcoin to reach $126,080 again, with 2028 more likely. The next halving is expected in April 2028, and historical trends show Bitcoin typically gains momentum in the 12 to 24 months after such events.

New Delhi, Nov 16 (PTI) After the success of “Black Warrant”, his bestselling account of Tihar jail’s most notorious executions and the hit web series it inspired, author Sunil Gupta returns with another gripping account of the prison’s dark history in his upcoming book, “Red Alert: Famous Jailbreaks of Tihar”.
Co-authored with journalist Samanwaya Rautray, the book, published by Hachette India, is scheduled for release on November 19.
Drawing on Gupta’s decades of experience within the prison system, “Red Alert” reconstructs some of Tihar jail’s most audacious escapes and the extensive manhunts that followed.
The book chronicles extraordinary jailbreaks, including the escape of 13 life convicts who allegedly spent weeks digging a 125-foot tunnel beneath the prison before disappearing into the night.
It also revisits the dramatic escape of serial killer Charles Sobhraj, who drugged guards and fellow inmates, took a hostage and managed to walk out of the high-security prison.
“Sher Singh Rana, convicted of assassinating Phoolan Devi, the ‘bandit queen’ turned politician, escapes so brazenly that Tihar is forced to overhaul its security,” reads the book’s description, recounting yet another jailbreak from Tihar.
Through these accounts, Gupta and Rautray explore the systemic failures that enabled the escapes, highlighting recurring issues of negligence, corruption, collusion and security lapses within an institution regarded as one of the most formidable prison complexes in Asia.
Despite Tihar’s reputation as a virtually escape-proof facility, the incidents reveal how its defences were breached repeatedly, raising questions about institutional accountability and the circumstances that allowed the escapes to take place.
The book, priced at Rs 599, is currently available for pre-order online. PTI MG MG
